# Pretraining and the Model Landscape {#sec-pretraining}

**Learning objectives.** After this chapter you can:

- draw the stages that turn a randomly initialised transformer into a
  deployable model, and say what data and what objective each stage uses;
- follow a token from a web crawl into a training batch, naming what each
  filtering step removes and what it is protecting against;
- explain why the most aggressive deduplication in an open dataset made the
  data *worse*, and what that tells you about quality filters in general;
- estimate any pretraining run's compute, wall-clock time, and rental bill
  from two numbers — and state exactly where that estimate stops being true;
- read model FLOPs utilization as the gap between a hardware brochure and a
  datacentre, and attribute the gap to the right cause;
- measure what a tokenizer costs a language, and price that cost in context
  window, in latency, and in money;
- classify a model release by what it actually opens — weights, data, code,
  licence — and choose one for a task and a budget.

## A model that can compute and knows nothing

At the end of @sec-transformers we had a machine with the right shape and no
contents. Every matrix in it — $W^Q$, $W^K$, $W^V$, $W_1$, $W_2$, the
embedding table — is full of small random numbers. The architecture is
finished. The model knows nothing. Ask a freshly initialised Llama-shaped
network to continue *kedi sütü* and it hands back a token drawn very nearly
uniformly from 128,000 possibilities, because that is what a softmax over
untrained scores does.

Everything the model will ever know arrives through one procedure, repeated a
few million times:

> show it a stretch of text, ask it to predict the next token, measure how
> wrong it was, and nudge every parameter slightly in the direction that would
> have made the true token more likely.

That is the whole mechanism. There is no second one. Grammar, the capital of
France, how to close a Python bracket, the fact that coffee can be ready and
robots take instructions — all of it is a side effect of getting better at
that one prediction, over enough text.

[This chapter is about what happens when you run that loop at industrial
scale.]{.hl} Where the text comes from, what has to be thrown away before it
is usable, what the run costs in hardware and hours and money, why a Turkish
sentence costs more than its English translation, and how to tell one model
release from another when every one of them is announced as state of the art.

### Three stages, and the first one dominates the data bill

A deployable assistant is not the output of one training run. It is the output
of a short pipeline, and [the stages differ in what they are *for*, not just
in how much data they consume]{.hl}.

The two things that matter about each stage are *what the data is* and *how
much of it there is*, and they point in opposite directions: the stage with
the most data has the least curation, and the stage with the most careful
curation has almost no data.
:::
::::

Put published numbers on that gap. GPT-3 was pretrained on 300 billion tokens
[@brown2020language]. The InstructGPT work that turned a GPT-3-class base
model into something you could talk to used about 13,000 supervised prompts —
12,725 in the training split, averaging 408 tokens each, so on the order of
five million tokens of prompt text — plus 33,000 prompts for the reward model
and 31,000 for the reinforcement-learning stage [@ouyang2022training].

[Pretraining saw roughly 58,000 times the *prompt* tokens that supervised
fine-tuning did.]{.hl} Read the denominator carefully: those five million tokens
are prompts only, and an SFT example is a prompt plus a response, with the loss
usually taken on the response. The ratio against the complete training text is
smaller, and neither paper reports it. Even so the order of magnitude is the most useful single fact about this pipeline,
because it explains a pattern you would otherwise find baffling: a fine-tune
reliably changes *how* a model answers, and moves *what it knows* only at the
margins. @sec-post-training measures both, and facts can be taught later — it is
just that a few million tokens against three hundred billion is not the place to
install a worldview, and retrieval is usually the easier way to keep facts
current. The bulk of the knowledge was installed in stage 1. Stages 2 and 3 are a coat of
paint — an important one, applied by skilled people, on a building someone
else spent tens of millions of dollars constructing.

::: {.column-margin}
The word *pretraining* is a historical accident. It was coined when the stage
really was preliminary: you pretrained on unlabelled text, then trained
properly on your labelled task. The proportions inverted and the name never
caught up.
:::

This chapter is about stage 1. @sec-post-training takes stages 2 and 3
seriously, including LoRA, DPO, and what "alignment" actually buys.

### Why the order cannot be swapped

It is worth being explicit about why you cannot skip to stage 2, since stage 2
is the one whose data you can actually afford.

The instruction data is far too small to teach a language.

Five million tokens is roughly forty novels. Nothing reaches an assistant's
command of English syntax — let alone Python semantics and the geography of
Anatolia — from forty novels. A model can certainly learn *something* from a
corpus that size; what it cannot do is acquire broad general competence there,
and a model with billions of parameters would mostly memorise them.

What five million carefully written tokens *can* do is teach a **format**.
That a question is followed by an answer rather than by another question. That
a request for a list produces a list. That *"I don't know"* is a permitted
output.

And format is cheap to learn precisely because the
[base model](#gloss-base-model){#term-base-model .term-ref} already has every ingredient. It simply had no reason to
prefer one arrangement over another.

::: {#gloss-base-model .column-margin .term-gloss}
**base model** — what pretraining produces on its own: something that continues text plausibly, with no particular reason to answer a question rather than ask another one. [↩](#term-base-model){.term-back}
:::

That is the cause and effect worth carrying:

| stage | supplies | costs | can it be redone? |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| pretraining | knowledge, grammar, world model | months, thousands of GPUs | in practice, never |
| fine-tuning | format, task shape, domain style | hours to days, one node | constantly |
| preference tuning | tone, refusals, ranking of answers | days, plus annotation | every release |
| RL on verifiable rewards | reasoning traces, tool use | days to weeks, a real cluster | every release |

**A fourth stage arrived after that picture was drawn.** Since late 2024, models
trained for reasoning add large-scale reinforcement learning against verifiable
rewards — maths with a checkable answer, code with a passing test — and that
stage does not fit the "coat of paint" description. Its token counts stay small,
but its *compute* does not: rollouts are generation, and generation is the
expensive half of RL. The 58,000× ratio above is a fact about **data**, not
about **dollars**, and @sec-reasoning is where the dollars go.

The last column is why this chapter matters even if you never train anything.
[The pretraining decisions are the ones you inherit and cannot undo.]{.hl} If
the tokenizer splits Turkish badly, every downstream user pays for it forever.
If the data cutoff is December 2023, later training *can* teach the model who
won an election in 2025 — you then own the coverage, the reliability and the
interference, which is why retrieval usually wins for facts that keep moving.
If the corpus contained little Turkish, an adapter has very little to build on.

**What we will look at.** What pretraining produces and — more usefully —
what it does not. Then the three decisions that consume the budget before any
architecture question arrives: where the text comes from, how it is cut into
tokens, and what the run actually costs. We finish with the landscape of
models you can choose from, and how to read a claim about one.

## Where the data comes from {#sec-pretraining-data}

The honest answer to "what is a large language model trained on?" is: the web,
plus whatever else the lab could obtain, minus an enormous amount that had to
be thrown away. The interesting part is the *minus*.

### The raw material

Almost every open pretraining corpus begins at [Common Crawl](#gloss-common-crawl){#term-common-crawl .term-ref}, a nonprofit
that has crawled the web since 2008 and publishes the results. It releases a
*snapshot* every month or two; the FineWeb team worked from 96 of them
[@penedo2024fineweb]. Each snapshot is a few hundred terabytes of raw HTTP
responses.

::: {#gloss-common-crawl .column-margin .term-gloss}
**Common Crawl** — a nonprofit that has crawled the public web since 2008 and publishes each crawl free of charge. Nearly every open pretraining corpus starts here. [↩](#term-common-crawl){.term-back}
:::

Two file formats matter, and choosing between them is the first real decision.
WARC files hold the raw HTML as served. WET files hold Common Crawl's own
plain-text extraction, which is free and saves an enormous amount of compute.
FineWeb used WARC and ran their own extraction with `trafilatura`, for a reason
they state plainly: [the WET files "retained too much boilerplate and menu
text"]{.hl} [@penedo2024fineweb]. Navigation bars, cookie notices, and footer
links are text, and a next-token objective will happily learn to predict them.

This is the first appearance of a pattern that runs through the entire
pipeline: *the model has no way to tell you its data was bad.* It minimises the
loss it is given. If a tenth of the achievable loss reduction lives in cookie
banners, it will become excellent at cookie banners.

### What each filter is actually protecting against

A list of filters is boring. The reason each one exists is not.

| filter | removes | the failure it prevents |
|:--|:--|:--|
| URL blocklist | pages on an adult-content list | training on material you cannot defend and cannot later remove |
| `trafilatura` extraction | navigation, ads, footers | a model fluent in "Accept all cookies" |
| fastText language ID, score $\ge 0.65$ | pages not confidently English | a corpus whose claimed language is not its actual language |
| repetition filters | pages that repeat one line 400 times | degenerate loops at generation time |
| quality heuristics | no terminal punctuation, absurd symbol ratios | keyword-stuffed spam no human ever read |
| MinHash deduplication | near-identical documents | memorisation, and compute spent twice on one text |
| PII reformatting | e-mail addresses, phone numbers | a model that can be prompted into leaking a real person's details |

Two of those rows deserve more than a table cell.

**Deduplication earns its place empirically.** Models trained on deduplicated
data memorise their training set substantially less, and are no worse
downstream [@lee2022deduplicating]. The memorisation is not hypothetical:
given the right prompt, a large model will emit long verbatim passages of its
training data, including personal information [@carlini2021extracting].
Duplicates make this worse for a mechanical reason — a passage that appears a
hundred times is a passage the gradient has rewarded the model a hundred times
for reproducing.

**The language filter is a policy, not a measurement.** A 0.65 threshold on an
English classifier does not merely *detect* language, it *defines* the corpus.
Code-switched text, Turkish written without diacritics, English with heavy
dialect features: all score lower, all get dropped. When a model is later found
weak on some variety of language, this is usually where it happened — silently,
months before anybody trained anything.

### The deduplication surprise

Now the result that should change how you think about data pipelines.

[Deduplication](#gloss-deduplication){#term-deduplication .term-ref} has an obvious knob: how widely do you look for
duplicates? Within one snapshot, or across all 96? Across all of them is more
thorough, so it ought to be better.

::: {#gloss-deduplication .column-margin .term-gloss}
**deduplication** — removing documents that are identical or near-identical to ones already kept, so the model does not spend compute on, or memorise, the same text repeatedly. [↩](#term-deduplication){.term-back}
:::

FineWeb tried exactly that. The two strategies are alternative routes from the
same starting point: run on the ~36 trillion tokens of base-filtered text,
per-snapshot deduplication leaves **20 trillion** and global deduplication
leaves **4 trillion** — a fifth as much, and roughly a ninth of what went in.
It also hit the oldest snapshots hardest, [removing "as much as 90% of the
original base filtered data"]{.hl} from them, since those had 95 later crawls
to be deduplicated against [@penedo2024fineweb].

Then they checked, which is the part most pipelines skip. Taking the 2013-48
snapshot in isolation, they built two *pools*: the ~31 billion tokens global
deduplication had **kept**, and 171 billion tokens re-deduplicated out of the
~460 billion it had **removed**. They then trained one ablation model on a
sample from each pool, at the same model size and the same token budget, so the
only variable was which pool the tokens came from. The kept pool lost.

That equal-budget detail is what makes the result mean anything. Had one model
simply seen more tokens than the other, the comparison would have measured data
*quantity* and told you nothing about data *quality*, which is the whole claim.

Their explanation, after reading documents by hand, is what to memorise: the
data surviving aggressive global deduplication "contains more ads, incoherent
lists of keywords and generally badly formatted text than originally removed
data" [@penedo2024fineweb].

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**Why this happens, and why it will happen to you.** The mechanism is worth
getting right, because the obvious explanation is wrong. Deduplication does
not throw away good writing — it keeps one copy of everything. What matters is
*which* copy it keeps. FineWeb deduplicated iteratively, starting from the
newest snapshot and working backwards, so every document that also appeared in
a later crawl was struck from the older ones. Good writing is exactly what gets
quoted, syndicated and mirrored forward in time, so it survives in the recent
snapshots and is stripped from the old ones. Spam is generated fresh and never
reappears, so it stays where it was.

Nothing good was deleted. But within any one old snapshot the *proportion* of
junk went up, and the paper says so directly: [global deduplication "upsamples
lower-quality data in the last deduplicated crawl, resulting in worse
performance of the retained data compared to the removed data"]{.hl}
[@penedo2024fineweb].

The general lesson: a proxy — here, duplication — was standing in for something
you actually wanted, and past a certain strength the proxy inverted. Nobody
would have caught this by reasoning about it. They caught it by training two
models and comparing.
:::

This is why FineWeb deduplicates *within* each snapshot and stops there. It is
also a preview of an argument that recurs throughout this book: when a data
decision looks obviously right, the cost of checking it with a small training
run is almost always lower than the cost of being wrong at scale.

### Quantity is not weight

Having collected data, you must decide how much of each kind the model
actually sees. These are different numbers, and conflating them is a classic
misreading of a model report.

GPT-3's table makes the distinction unusually clear [@brown2020language]:

| dataset | tokens available | share of the training mix | times seen in 300B tokens |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|
| Common Crawl (filtered) | 410B | 60% | 0.44 |
| WebText2 | 19B | 22% | 2.9 |
| Books1 | 12B | 8% | 1.9 |
| Books2 | 55B | 8% | 0.43 |
| Wikipedia | 3B | 3% | 3.4 |

Read the last two columns together. Wikipedia is **0.6%** of the available
tokens and **3%** of the training mix, so the model went through the whole of
Wikipedia 3.4 times while reading less than half of the filtered web crawl.
The authors say why in one sentence: the weights are deliberately *not*
proportional to size, and they accept "a small amount of overfitting in
exchange for higher quality training data" [@brown2020language].

Two bookkeeping notes before you reuse this table. The mix column is the
paper's own rounded figures and sums to 101%, not 100%. And the last column is
the paper's reported epoch count, not something you can recompute from the
other two: share × 300B ÷ tokens available gives 3.5 for WebText2 against the
2.9 printed, and 3.0 for Wikipedia against the 3.4 printed. These are the
figures the original table reports; they do not reconcile exactly, and rounded
shares are not enough to establish why. Read the table for the *shape* of the
argument — quantity
is not weight — and not as a set of numbers that close.

Four years later Llama 3 reports its mixture by *topic* rather than by source,
which itself tells you what the field learned to care about: roughly [50%
general knowledge, 25% mathematical and reasoning tokens, 17% code, and 8%
multilingual]{.hl} [@grattafiori2024llama3]. Note the last figure. Eight
percent, shared across every language that is not English, in a model
explicitly marketed as multilingual. Keep that number — it returns when we
price what Turkish costs.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**Code is not in there for the coding.** Seventeen percent of a
general-purpose model's diet being source code looks odd until you consider
what code *is*: long-range structured text in which a mistake thousands of
tokens earlier makes the continuation invalid. It is the most reliably
self-checking text on the internet. Whether it is *causally* responsible for
better reasoning is still argued; that labs keep raising the proportion tells
you what they believe.
:::

### The last forty million tokens

Llama 3's pretraining is itself three stages, and the proportions are
startling [@grattafiori2024llama3]:

1. **Initial pretraining.** AdamW, peak learning rate $8\times10^{-5}$, warmed
   up over 8,000 steps, decayed on a cosine schedule to $8\times10^{-7}$ over
   1.2 million steps. The batch size *grows*: 4M tokens at sequence length
   4,096, doubled to 8M tokens at length 8,192 after 252M tokens, doubled
   again to 16M after 2.87 trillion tokens. Small batches early buy stability;
   large batches later buy efficiency.
2. **Long-context pretraining.** The context window is raised from 8K to 128K
   in six stages, using roughly 800 billion tokens — about 5% of the whole run
   spent purely on learning to use a longer window.
3. **Annealing.** Over the **final 40 million tokens** the learning rate is
   taken linearly to zero while the data mix shifts to upsample very
   high-quality sources. The released weights are then a Polyak average of
   checkpoints from this phase.

Forty million tokens is $0.00026\%$ of 15.6 trillion. And it matters: on the
8B model, [annealing](#gloss-annealing){#term-annealing .term-ref} on high-quality code and mathematics improved GSM8k by
24.0% and MATH by 6.4%. On the 405B model the same treatment was negligible,
which the authors read as the larger model already having the capability and
not needing the reminder.

::: {#gloss-annealing .column-margin .term-gloss}
**annealing** — taking the learning rate down to zero at the end of a run, usually while shifting the data mix toward the best material available. Borrowed from metallurgy, where slow cooling settles a structure. [↩](#term-annealing){.term-back}
:::

[Where a token sits in the schedule changes what it teaches.]{.hl} A token
seen at step 400,000 under a large learning rate contributes to a broad
capability that a million later gradients will partly overwrite. A token seen
in the last 0.0003% of the run, as the learning rate goes to zero, lands in
weights that will never move again. That mechanism is behind an otherwise
mysterious industrial habit: save the best data for last.

### How many times may you reuse a token?

Sooner or later every serious pretraining project runs out of the language it
wants. This is already true for Turkish, and it will be true for English
sooner than the raw token counts suggest. The obvious move is more [epochs](#gloss-epoch){#term-epoch .term-ref} over
what you have.

::: {#gloss-epoch .column-margin .term-gloss}
**epoch** — one complete pass over the training data. Frontier pretraining runs are usually well under one epoch; the question here is what happens when you are forced above it. [↩](#term-epoch){.term-back}
:::

The measured answer is more generous than folklore expects
[@muennighoff2023scaling]. Training on [up to four epochs of repeated data
"yields negligible changes to loss compared to having unique data"]{.hl}. Past
that, the value of each further epoch decays — and eventually the value of
adding *compute* decays to zero as well, because extra passes over data the
model has already exhausted cannot help.

The practical shape of the advice:

| your situation | what the evidence supports |
|:--|:--|
| more unique tokens available than compute | use unique data; never repeat |
| data-limited, modest compute overrun | repeat up to about 4 epochs, nearly free |
| data-limited, large compute overrun | split it between parameters *and* epochs, tilting toward epochs |
| far past both limits | stop; the extra compute is buying nothing |

The third row is the one that surprises people, so take it from the authors
directly: in the data-constrained regime, [allocating new compute to "both more
parameters and epochs is necessary, and … epochs should be scaled slightly
faster"]{.hl} [@muennighoff2023scaling]. Their figure puts it more sharply
still — the data suggest "training smaller models for more epochs, in contrast
to what assuming Chinchilla scaling laws hold for repeated data would predict".
If you reach for Chinchilla's ratio when you are short of data, it will tell
you to buy parameters, and it will be wrong.

For a Turkish project this is genuinely liberating. A corpus of 30 billion
Turkish tokens does not cap you at 30 billion tokens of training; it is closer
to 120 billion before returns visibly bend, which changes what model size is
defensible.

## The tokenizer is a budget decision {#sec-tokenizer-budget}

One pretraining decision is made before the first gradient step, is never
revisited, and silently taxes every user of the model for its entire life. It
is the tokenizer.

@sec-text-as-data introduced subword tokenization as a way to avoid an
unbounded vocabulary. That framing is correct and incomplete. At pretraining
scale the tokenizer is not a preprocessing convenience — [it is how the
compute budget gets divided between languages]{.hl}, and the division is
permanent for practical purposes. An ordinary fine-tune leaves the segmentation
exactly where it was; replacing it is a separate project, with its own cost,
described in @sec-pretraining-interview.

Llama 3's tokenizer is a good example of the decision being made explicitly.
Its 128,000-token vocabulary is 100,000 tokens taken from OpenAI's `tiktoken`
plus [28,000 added specifically to support non-English
languages]{.hl} [@grattafiori2024llama3]. The report notes that these 28K
improved compression and downstream performance for other languages "with no
impact on English tokenization". That is a design *choice*, with a price tag,
made once.

### Fertility, and why the obvious metric lies

The standard measure is [fertility](#gloss-fertility){#term-fertility .term-ref}: tokens per word. Lower is better.

::: {#gloss-fertility .column-margin .term-gloss}
**fertility** — how many tokens a tokenizer produces per word of input. Meaningful when comparing two tokenizers on one language; misleading when comparing two languages, as the next paragraph shows. [↩](#term-fertility){.term-back}
:::

For Turkish, fertility is the wrong number, and getting this wrong will make
you draw a conclusion that is exactly backwards. Turkish is agglutinative: it
stacks suffixes onto a stem, so one Turkish word routinely carries what
English needs four or five words to say. *Evlerinizden* is one word and means
"from your houses". Comparing tokens-per-word across the two languages
compares units of different size.

The honest measurement is **tokens for the same content**: take a sentence and
its professional translation, tokenize both, and divide. That ratio is what a
Turkish user actually pays — in context window, in latency, and on every API
invoice.

### The measurement

We ran both metrics over a real parallel corpus rather than a hand-picked
paragraph, because a single passage can be a fluke. The source is the
`en-tr` portion of OPUS-100, from which 3,000 sentence pairs were downloaded
and filtered down to 1,157 usable ones: both sides at least four words, and a
character-length ratio between 0.4 and 2.5, which drops the misalignments
that machine-built parallel corpora always contain. That leaves 8,058 Turkish
words against 10,862 English words of matched content — and note that
disparity, because it *is* the agglutination showing up in the raw counts.

Every number below comes from running the tokenizer that actually ships with
the model — `openai-community/gpt2`,
`google-bert/bert-base-multilingual-cased`, `NousResearch/Meta-Llama-3-8B`,
`Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B`, `dbmdz/bert-base-turkish-cased`, and
`ytu-ce-cosmos/turkish-gpt2`.

| tokenizer | vocab | TR/word | EN/word | same content | median |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| GPT-2 (2019) | 50,257 | 3.42 | 1.28 | **1.98×** | 1.92 |
| BERT multilingual (2018) | 119,547 | 2.38 | 1.43 | **1.23×** | 1.21 |
| Llama 3 (2024) | 128,000 | 2.12 | 1.28 | **1.23×** | 1.22 |
| Qwen 2.5 (2024) | 151,643 | 2.43 | 1.29 | **1.40×** | 1.39 |
| BERTurk (Turkish-native) | 32,000 | 1.59 | 2.03 | **0.58×** | 0.58 |
| Cosmos GPT-2 (Turkish-native) | 50,257 | 1.56 | 1.79 | **0.64×** | 0.64 |

The "same content" column is the aggregate ratio over the whole corpus; the
"median" is the median of the per-sentence ratios over the first 800 pairs,
computed separately so that one long outlier cannot drive the headline. For
five of the six tokenizers the two agree to within 0.02, which is the sanity
check that the aggregate is not an artefact. GPT-2 is the exception, at 1.98
against 1.92. Resist reading a length effect into that gap. The aggregate is a
length-weighted mean of the per-sentence ratios, and a weighted mean can sit
above a median without any relationship to length at all: three equal-length
sentences with ratios 1, 1 and 2 give an aggregate of 1.33 against a median of
1. The two figures also come from different samples here — 1,157 pairs against
the first 800. Testing whether GPT-2's Turkish penalty grows with sentence
length means plotting the per-sentence ratio against length on one common set of
pairs, which this table does not do.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof fertMetric = Inputs.radio(
  [
    "Tokens for the same content (Turkish ÷ English)",
    "Tokens per word (the misleading view)"
  ],
  { value: "Tokens for the same content (Turkish ÷ English)", label: "" }
)
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
fertRows = [
  { name: "GPT-2 (2019)",              vocab:  50257, tr: 3.42, en: 1.28, same: 1.98 },
  { name: "Qwen 2.5 (2024)",           vocab: 151643, tr: 2.43, en: 1.29, same: 1.40 },
  { name: "BERT multiling. (2018)",    vocab: 119547, tr: 2.38, en: 1.43, same: 1.23 },
  { name: "Llama 3 (2024)",            vocab: 128000, tr: 2.12, en: 1.28, same: 1.23 },
  { name: "Cosmos GPT-2 (TR-native)",  vocab:  50257, tr: 1.56, en: 1.79, same: 0.64 },
  { name: "BERTurk (TR-native)",       vocab:  32000, tr: 1.59, en: 2.03, same: 0.58 }
]
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
fertOrder = fertRows.map(d => d.name)
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
fertPlot = {
  const sameMode = fertMetric.startsWith("Tokens for the same");

  if (sameMode) {
    return Plot.plot({
      width: 700,
      height: 320,
      marginLeft: 190,
      marginRight: 40,
      x: { label: "Turkish tokens per English token, same content →", domain: [0, 2.2], grid: true },
      y: { domain: fertOrder, label: null },
      marks: [
        Plot.barX(fertRows, {
          y: "name",
          x: "same",
          fill: d => d.same > 1 ? "#C1666B" : "#0E7C7B",
          rx: 3,
          title: d => `${d.name}: ${d.same.toFixed(2)}x`
        }),
        Plot.text(fertRows, {
          y: "name",
          x: "same",
          text: d => d.same.toFixed(2) + "x",
          dx: 16,
          fontWeight: "bold"
        }),
        Plot.ruleX([1], { stroke: "currentColor", strokeDasharray: "4 3" }),
        Plot.ruleX([0])
      ]
    });
  }

  const long = fertRows.flatMap(d => [
    { name: d.name, lang: "Turkish", v: d.tr },
    { name: d.name, lang: "English", v: d.en }
  ]);

  return Plot.plot({
    width: 700,
    height: 380,
    marginLeft: 190,
    marginRight: 40,
    x: { label: "tokens per word →", domain: [0, 3.7], grid: true },
    fy: { domain: fertOrder, label: null },
    y: { domain: ["Turkish", "English"], axis: null },
    color: {
      domain: ["Turkish", "English"],
      range: ["#C1666B", "#1F4E79"],
      legend: true
    },
    marks: [
      Plot.barX(long, {
        fy: "name",
        y: "lang",
        x: "v",
        fill: "lang",
        rx: 2,
        title: d => `${d.name} — ${d.lang}: ${d.v.toFixed(2)} tokens/word`
      }),
      Plot.ruleX([0])
    ]
  });
}
```

Switch between the two views and watch the two Turkish-native tokenizers.
Under tokens-per-word they look like the clear winners on Turkish and it is
not obvious what they lose. Under the same-content ratio the trade appears:
they are *below* 1.0 on Turkish because they are paying for it on English,
where they need 1.8 to 2.0 tokens per word against Llama 3's 1.28.

### Three things the table says

**1. The gap narrowed enormously, and it was engineering, not luck.** GPT-2
charged Turkish a 98% surcharge — the same content cost almost exactly twice
as many tokens. Llama 3 charges 23%. Nothing about Turkish changed between
2019 and 2024. What changed is that tokenizer training data stopped being
overwhelmingly English.

**2. Vocabulary size is not the lever.** This is the finding that surprises
people, and it falls straight out of the table. Qwen 2.5 has a *larger*
vocabulary than Llama 3 — 151,643 against 128,000 — and is *worse* on Turkish:
1.40× against 1.23×. A bigger vocabulary spent on other languages does nothing
for yours. [What matters is not how many slots the vocabulary has but what the
corpus that trained it contained.]{.hl}

**3. A 32K Turkish-native vocabulary beats a 128K multilingual one on
Turkish.** BERTurk gets 0.58× with a quarter of Llama 3's vocabulary. It also
needs 2.03 tokens per English word, which is roughly GPT-2's Turkish
performance in reverse. There is no free lunch here and no "better tokenizer"
in the abstract: a vocabulary is a fixed budget, and every slot given to
Turkish morphology is a slot not given to English, code, or Chinese.

### Look at what actually happens to a word

Ratios hide the mechanism. Here is one long but perfectly ordinary Turkish
word — *bilgisayarlaştırabildiklerimizden*, "from the ones we were able to
computerise" — cut three ways.

::: {.fig-cap}
Segmentations produced by running each tokenizer, not by hand. Llama 3's nine
pieces cost 2.25 times what the Turkish-native tokenizer's four do — for one
word, in every forward pass, forever.
:::
::::

Look at where Llama 3 cuts. It splits *bilgisayar* — an ordinary everyday
noun, "computer" — into `bil | gis | ayar`, three fragments, none of which is
a Turkish morpheme and one of which (`ayar`, "setting, adjustment") is an
unrelated real word. The model must reassemble the concept from pieces every
single time it appears.

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**Fewer tokens is not the same as better linguistics, and the difference
matters.** On *evlerinizden* ("from your houses") Llama 3 produces
`ev | ler | iniz | den` — exactly the four morphemes, a textbook
segmentation. The Turkish-native Cosmos tokenizer produces
`ev | lerinizden`: two tokens, cheaper, and blind to the internal structure,
since `lerinizden` spans three morphemes rather than being one.

So the two metrics genuinely can disagree. Compression is what you pay for
and is easy to measure. Morphological alignment is what might help the model
generalise to a suffix combination it has not seen, and is hard to measure.
Do not assume the cheaper segmentation is the more linguistically sensible
one — check, as we just did.
:::

### What the surcharge actually costs

Take the measured corpus figure for Llama 3: Turkish costs **1.23×** the
tokens of English for identical content. That single number propagates into
four separate bills.

| where it lands | the effect at 1.23× |
|:--|:--|
| context window | a 128,000-token window holds about 104,000 English-equivalent tokens of Turkish |
| API cost | one million English-equivalent tokens costs the price of 1.23 million |
| latency | generation is per token, so at the same tokens-per-second a Turkish answer takes about 23% longer |
| pretraining compute | at fixed FLOPs, a Turkish corpus buys about 19% less content than an English one |

Watch the direction of that last number, because it is the single easiest
mistake to make with a ratio. Turkish costs 1.23× *more* tokens, but a fixed
token budget buys $1/1.23 = 0.813$ of the content — **18.7% less**, not 23%
less. The two are not the same figure, and only the API-cost and latency rows multiply by 1.23; the context-window and compute rows divide by it. That is why
128,000 tokens holds about 104,000 English-equivalent tokens rather than 98,560.

The compute row is the one that compounds. From @sec-scaling-laws, compute
scales with the token count, so a fixed budget spent on Turkish sees roughly a
fifth less *material* than the same budget spent on English — fewer facts,
fewer sentences, fewer patterns, for exactly the same money. The tokenizer tax
is not only charged at inference. It was charged during pretraining, to the
model you are now using.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**Measure this for your own language and your own text before you commit.** It
takes about fifteen lines. Take a few hundred sentence pairs of your domain
text and its translation, run every tokenizer you are considering over both
sides, and divide. Domain matters as much as language: legal Turkish, clinical
Turkish, and Turkish social media do not tokenize alike, and a corpus average
will not warn you.
:::

Under 1.23× the pragmatic answer is usually "use the multilingual model
anyway" — 23% is real but it does not overturn a decision. Under GPT-2's
1.98× it does. That is precisely why you measure instead of assuming, and the
full decision, including when a Turkish-native model wins outright, is
@sec-turkish-nlp's subject.

## What a run costs {#sec-pretraining-compute}

You can estimate the compute of any pretraining run — how many
[FLOPs](#gloss-flop){#term-flop .term-ref} it consumed — from two numbers, the
parameter count $N$ and the token count $D$. For the matrix multiplies that
dominate, the estimate is good to well under a percent — attention is the term
it leaves out, and this section comes back to when that matters. That is unusual enough in systems work to be worth taking seriously,
and it is the tool that lets you sanity-check a press release.

**One caveat first, because it decides which number you put in $N$.** The $6ND$
rule counts operations per parameter *used*, and in a mixture-of-experts model (@sec-transformers)
a token only touches the experts its router picked
[@jiang2024mixtral]. So the figure you want is active parameters, not total:

$$C \approx 6\,N_{\text{active}}\,D$$

DeepSeek-V3 makes the gap concrete: 671B total parameters, about 37B active per
token, 14.8T training tokens. Using the active count gives
$6 \times 37{\times}10^{9} \times 14.8{\times}10^{12} \approx 3.3\times10^{24}$
FLOPs; substituting the total would have over-counted by **18×**. Whenever a
release quotes two parameter counts, the smaller one is the one this
arithmetic wants.

::: {#gloss-flop .column-margin .term-gloss}
**FLOP** — one floating-point operation: a single multiply or a single add on decimal numbers. Training compute is counted in FLOPs; chips are rated in FLOP/s, operations per second. The two are easy to confuse and differ by a factor of however long you ran. [↩](#term-flop){.term-back}
:::

### Where the 6 comes from

$$
C \;\approx\; 6\,N\,D \quad \text{FLOPs}
$$

The 6 is not a fudge factor. It is three twos, and each two has a cause.

:::: {.anlp-fig}
```{=html}
<div class="fig-title">Six floating-point operations per parameter per token</div>
<svg viewBox="0 0 764 320" style="max-width:744px" role="img"
     aria-label="Three panels explaining the constant six. The first panel, the forward pass, costs two operations per parameter per token: one multiply and one add, because every weight is used once in a multiply-accumulate. The second panel, the backward pass computing gradients with respect to the layer input so the error can travel further back, costs another two. The third panel, the backward pass computing gradients with respect to the weights themselves so the optimiser knows what to change, costs another two. A stacked bar at the bottom shows the forward pass is one third of the total cost and the backward pass is two thirds, which is the standard rule that backward costs about twice forward.">
  <rect x="14" y="34" width="236" height="128" rx="10" class="box-accent"/>
  <text x="132" y="58" class="t-xs t-mid t-b t-accent">FORWARD</text>
  <text x="132" y="84" class="t-sm t-mid t-b">2 per parameter</text>
  <text x="132" y="106" class="t-xs t-mid t-muted">every weight is used once in</text>
  <text x="132" y="120" class="t-xs t-mid t-muted">a multiply-accumulate:</text>
  <text x="132" y="140" class="t-xs t-mid t-mono">one × and one +</text>

  <rect x="264" y="34" width="236" height="128" rx="10" class="box-warm"/>
  <text x="382" y="58" class="t-xs t-mid t-b t-warm">BACKWARD — INPUT</text>
  <text x="382" y="84" class="t-sm t-mid t-b">2 per parameter</text>
  <text x="382" y="106" class="t-xs t-mid t-muted">the error has to keep travelling</text>
  <text x="382" y="120" class="t-xs t-mid t-muted">to earlier layers:</text>
  <text x="382" y="140" class="t-xs t-mid t-mono">∂L/∂x</text>

  <rect x="514" y="34" width="236" height="128" rx="10" class="box-warm"/>
  <text x="632" y="58" class="t-xs t-mid t-b t-warm">BACKWARD — WEIGHTS</text>
  <text x="632" y="84" class="t-sm t-mid t-b">2 per parameter</text>
  <text x="632" y="106" class="t-xs t-mid t-muted">the optimiser needs to know</text>
  <text x="632" y="120" class="t-xs t-mid t-muted">what to change:</text>
  <text x="632" y="140" class="t-xs t-mid t-mono">∂L/∂W</text>

  <text x="60" y="204" class="t-xs t-b t-muted">SHARE OF THE TOTAL</text>
  <rect x="60"  y="214" width="220" height="34" rx="5" class="box-accent"/>
  <text x="170" y="236" class="t-xs t-mid t-b">forward — 2ND</text>
  <rect x="284" y="214" width="436" height="34" rx="5" class="box-warm"/>
  <text x="502" y="236" class="t-xs t-mid t-b">backward — 4ND</text>

  <text x="60" y="278" class="t-xs t-muted">This is why "the backward pass costs about twice the forward pass" is a rule of thumb</text>
  <text x="60" y="294" class="t-xs t-muted">rather than a measurement: it is what the chain rule requires, not what a profiler found.</text>
</svg>
```
::: {.fig-cap}
Two for the forward pass, four for the backward pass, once per parameter per
token. Multiply by $N$ parameters and $D$ tokens and you have the run.
:::
::::

The forward two is the easy one. Every weight in a matrix multiply gets used
exactly once per token: one multiplication and one addition into the
accumulator. Two operations, per weight, per token.

The backward four is where people lose the thread, so name the two jobs
separately. Backpropagation through a layer must produce *two* different
gradients. It needs $\partial L/\partial x$ — how the loss changes with the
layer's *input* — or the error cannot propagate to the layer below. And it
needs $\partial L/\partial W$ — how the loss changes with each *weight* — or
the optimiser has nothing to update. Each of those is another matrix multiply
of the same shape, so each costs another 2 per parameter per token. Two jobs,
two each, four total.

### Does it agree with what the labs publish?

| run | $N$ | $D$ | $6ND$ | published | difference |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| GPT-3 | 175B | 300B | $3.150\times10^{23}$ | $3.14\times10^{23}$ | +0.32% |
| Llama 3 405B | 405B | 15.6T | $3.791\times10^{25}$ | $3.80\times10^{25}$ | −0.24% |

Under half a percent, across a factor of 120 in compute and four years of
architecture change. It is tempting to call this a validation of the law. It is
not, and the distinction matters more than the agreement does.

[Those published figures are themselves $6ND$.]{.hl} GPT-3's Appendix D prints
the arithmetic in columns — "Fwd-pass flops per active param per token: 2",
"Mult for bwd pass: 3", "Flops per param per token: 6" — and states the
assumption openly: "we ignore the attention operation, as it typically uses
less than 10% of the total compute for the models we are analyzing"
[@brown2020language]. Llama 3's $3.8\times10^{25}$ is likewise a *budget*: the
number Meta fixed in advance and then chose a model size to fit
[@grattafiori2024llama3].

So the table shows that our bookkeeping matches theirs, which is worth
confirming and is all it is. The reason to trust $6ND$ is the derivation in the
figure above, not this table. What the table does buy you is practical: since
the labs count this way, you can read any announcement that gives parameters
and tokens and reconstruct the number they would quote — and, as the next
section shows, know exactly what that number leaves out.

### Where it stops being true

$6ND$ counts the matrix multiplies whose cost is proportional to parameters.
Attention's score matrix is not one of those: it depends on the *sequence
length*, which appears nowhere in $N$ or $D$.

@sec-attention-cost gives attention's forward cost for a whole sequence as
$4n^2d$ per layer. Three steps turn that into a per-token figure: divide by $n$
to get $4nd$ per token, halve it because causal masking means the average
position attends to only half the sequence, then multiply by 3 because the
backward pass costs twice the forward. That leaves about $6\,L\,n\,d$ per token
for $L$ layers, sequence length $n$, and width $d$.

How much does ignoring it matter? Exactly as much as your context is long.

| model and context | $6N$ per token | attention per token | attention as share of $6N$ | true cost ÷ $6ND$ |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Llama 3 8B at 8K context | $4.82\times10^{10}$ | $6.44\times10^{9}$ | 13% | 1.13× |
| Llama 3 8B at 128K context | $4.82\times10^{10}$ | $1.03\times10^{11}$ | 214% | 3.14× |
| Llama 3 405B at 8K context | $2.43\times10^{12}$ | $1.02\times10^{11}$ | 4% | 1.04× |

Read the last column as "what you should multiply $6ND$ by to get the truth".

::: {.column-margin}
There is a smaller error pushing the other way. The input embedding is a
*lookup*, not a matrix multiply, so it costs essentially no FLOPs — yet its
parameters are counted in $N$. Llama 3's untied embedding is $128{,}256
\times 4096 = 525$M parameters, **6.5%** of the 8B's $N$ but only 1.5% of the
70B's and 0.5% of the 405B's. So $6ND$ over-counts small models slightly at
the same time as it under-counts attention. For the 8B at 8K the two partly
cancel.
:::

Two lessons, both practical. First, [$6ND$ is a *pretraining* law]{.hl}: it is
accurate because pretraining runs at short context, and the 405B is the most
accurate case of all because a wide model buries the attention term. Second,
at 128K context the true cost is more than three times what the law says —
which is precisely why long-context training is done as a short separate stage
on a fraction of the tokens rather than for the whole run.

### One run, end to end

Take Llama 3.1 405B and follow it from parameters to an invoice. Every input
is published: the paper gives $N$ and $D$, Meta's model card gives the
GPU-hours [@grattafiori2024llama3].

| quantity | value | where it comes from |
|:--|--:|:--|
| parameters | 405B | the paper |
| training tokens | 15.6T | the paper |
| compute | $3.79\times10^{25}$ FLOPs | $6ND$ |
| H100-hours | 30.84M | Meta's model card |
| on 8,000 H100s | 160.6 days | 30.84M ÷ 8,000 ÷ 24 |
| on 16,000 H100s | 80.3 days | the fleet actually used |
| on 24,000 H100s | 53.5 days | |
| rented at \$2.00/GPU-hour | ≈ \$62M | market rate, varies wildly |
| rented at \$3.00/GPU-hour | ≈ \$93M | |

Meta's card puts the whole Llama 3.1 family at **39.3M H100-hours**: 1.46M for
the 8B, 7.0M for the 70B, and 30.84M for the 405B. The 405B alone is 78% of
the family's compute.

::: {.column-margin}
Nobody rents 16,000 H100s by the hour, so the dollar figures are an
*opportunity cost*, not a bill Meta paid. They are still the right number for
you, because renting is exactly how you would reproduce any of this.
:::

### The brochure and the datacentre

Now the number that separates people who have run a cluster from people who
have read about one.

An H100 SXM is rated at **989 TFLOP/s** for dense BF16. (You will also see
1,979, which is the same chip with 2:4 structured sparsity — a different
operation that pretraining does not use. The PCIe card is a third slower again.
Check which number you are being quoted before comparing anything.) Divide the
FLOPs a run needed by the FLOPs its GPUs could have
produced in the hours it was allocated, and you get [model FLOPs
utilization](#gloss-model-flops-utilization){#term-model-flops-utilization .term-ref}: the fraction of the theoretical peak that actually became
training.

::: {#gloss-model-flops-utilization .column-margin .term-gloss}
**model FLOPs utilization** — the share of a chip's rated peak throughput that a real training run achieves, usually written *MFU*. Above 50% is rare; the gap is communication, memory bandwidth, and downtime. [↩](#term-model-flops-utilization){.term-back}
:::

The Llama 3 paper reports instantaneous BF16 MFU of **43%** on 8,000 GPUs,
**41%** on 16,000, and **38%** during the 128K-context stage
[@grattafiori2024llama3]. Here is what falls out of the published GPU-hours:

| model | GPU-hours | $6ND$ | effective MFU |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|
| Llama 3.1 8B | 1.46M | $7.23\times10^{23}$ | 13.9% |
| Llama 3.1 70B | 7.00M | $6.35\times10^{24}$ | 25.5% |
| Llama 3.1 405B | 30.84M | $3.79\times10^{25}$ | 34.5% |

::: {.column-margin}
The 8B and 70B token counts come from the card's prose, "~15 trillion
tokens" — its spec table says "15T+" for the same runs. Only the 405B's 15.6T
is stated precisely, and only in the paper. A few percent of slack in $D$ does not
change the picture.
:::

Look at the 405B row against the paper's own 41%. The run delivered 34.5%.
Where did the missing 6.5 points go? Two places, and it is worth separating
them, because one is a fact about datacentres and the other is a fact about
our own arithmetic.

**Most of it is probably downtime.** The paper says so in a sentence that is
easy to skim past. During a 54-day snapshot of pretraining there were **466 job
interruptions** — 47 planned, 419 unexpected — and the run sustained ">90%
effective training time" [@grattafiori2024llama3]. Take that bound as exactly
0.90 and apply one stage's 41% to the whole run, and:

$$
41\% \times 0.90 = 36.9\%
$$

Both of those are choices, so 36.9% is an illustrative figure rather than a
number the paper reports. On that reading it would account for **4.1** of the
6.5 points. Not bad kernels, not a weak
framework, not incompetence. Hardware fails, a node drops out, the job
restarts from the last checkpoint and redoes work. At 16,000 GPUs running for
weeks, something breaking every three hours is not a crisis — it is the
weather.

**The rest looks like our own accounting, not the cluster's.** We estimated the
numerator as $6ND$, and $6ND$ omits attention. The paper's MFU counts every FLOP the run
actually issued, including the attention matrices; our numerator does not. We
are comparing two different measurements and calling the difference waste.
Add attention back, using the $6Lnd$-per-token correction we derived above and
the paper's own schedule — 8K context for the bulk of the run, then
"approximately 800B training tokens" ramping through six stages to 128K
[@grattafiori2024llama3]:

| model | $6ND$ only | attention-corrected | 41% $\times\,0.90$, illustrative |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|
| Llama 3.1 8B | 13.9% | 15.8–17.2% | not published |
| Llama 3.1 70B | 25.5% | 27.4–29.0% | not published |
| Llama 3.1 405B | 34.5% | **36.0–37.1%** | **36.9%** |

The ranges bracket the long-context tail: the low end assumes it all ran at
8K, the high end at the full 128K, and the truth is somewhere between because
the context grew in stages. Only the 405B has a published MFU to check
against — the paper's Table 4 covers "each stage of Llama 3 405B
pre-training" and says nothing about the smaller runs. [For that one model the
corrected figure lands on the paper's number from either end of the
range]{.hl}: a bracket of 36.0–37.1% around a predicted 36.9%, which is as
close as this kind of reconstruction gets. The brochure, the paper, and the
invoice agree once you stop comparing apples to oranges.

::: {.column-margin}
The same Table 4 reports **430 TFLOP/s per GPU** at the 43% stage. $430/989 =
43.5\%$ — which confirms the paper is quoting against the *dense* 989 peak,
not the sparsity number. Always worth checking.
:::

Two lessons, and the second is the one that will save you: interruptions are a
real and large tax that no amount of kernel tuning removes, and **an MFU
number means nothing until you know what went in the numerator.** When a
vendor quotes you utilization, ask.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**Why the 8B still looks so much worse.** The attention correction lifts the
8B only to 15.8–17.2%, still less than half the 405B's. That is not the same
phenomenon and should not be explained the same way. Small models are harder
to keep an accelerator busy with: less arithmetic per unit of communication,
less work to hide latency behind, and a parallelism layout tuned for a 405B
sibling sharing the same cluster. The published GPU-hours are also *allocated*
hours, which include evaluation, checkpointing, and idle time that the paper's
instantaneous figure excludes — and with no published MFU for the 8B run there
is nothing to check the reconstruction against. Treat the 8B row as an upper
bound on waste, not a measurement of kernel quality — and treat the general
pattern as reliable: [big runs are efficient per GPU, small runs are
not]{.hl}.
:::

### Estimate your own run

Everything above is four multiplications. Change the inputs and watch which
one dominates.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof preN = Inputs.range([0.1, 500], { value: 8, step: 0.1, label: "Parameters (billions)" })
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof preD = Inputs.range([1, 20000], { value: 300, step: 1, label: "Training tokens (billions)" })
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof preMfu = Inputs.range([5, 60], { value: 35, step: 1, label: "Effective MFU (%)" })
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof preGpu = Inputs.select(
  ["H100 BF16 dense — 989 TFLOP/s", "A100 BF16 — 312 TFLOP/s", "H200 BF16 dense — 989 TFLOP/s"],
  { value: "H100 BF16 dense — 989 TFLOP/s", label: "Accelerator" }
)
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof preFleet = Inputs.range([8, 32000], { value: 512, step: 8, label: "GPUs in the fleet" })
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof prePrice = Inputs.range([0.5, 8], { value: 2.5, step: 0.1, label: "Rental price per GPU-hour (USD)" })
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
preCalc = {
  const peak = preGpu.startsWith("A100") ? 312e12 : 989e12;
  const N = preN * 1e9;
  const D = preD * 1e9;
  const flops = 6 * N * D;
  const gpuSeconds = flops / (peak * (preMfu / 100));
  const gpuHours = gpuSeconds / 3600;
  const days = gpuHours / preFleet / 24;
  const dollars = gpuHours * prePrice;
  const perParam = D / N;
  return { flops, gpuHours, days, dollars, perParam, peak };
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
html`<table style="width:100%; border-collapse:collapse; font-size:0.95rem">
  <tr><td style="padding:6px 10px">compute</td>
      <td style="padding:6px 10px; text-align:right; font-weight:600">${preCalc.flops.toExponential(2)} FLOPs</td></tr>
  <tr><td style="padding:6px 10px">GPU-hours</td>
      <td style="padding:6px 10px; text-align:right; font-weight:600">${
        preCalc.gpuHours >= 1e6
          ? (preCalc.gpuHours / 1e6).toFixed(2) + "M"
          : Math.round(preCalc.gpuHours).toLocaleString("en-US")
      }</td></tr>
  <tr><td style="padding:6px 10px">wall clock on ${preFleet.toLocaleString("en-US")} GPUs</td>
      <td style="padding:6px 10px; text-align:right; font-weight:600">${
        preCalc.days < 1
          ? (preCalc.days * 24).toFixed(1) + " hours"
          : preCalc.days.toFixed(1) + " days"
      }</td></tr>
  <tr><td style="padding:6px 10px">rental cost</td>
      <td style="padding:6px 10px; text-align:right; font-weight:600">${
        preCalc.dollars >= 1e6
          ? "$" + (preCalc.dollars / 1e6).toFixed(1) + "M"
          : "$" + Math.round(preCalc.dollars).toLocaleString("en-US")
      }</td></tr>
  <tr><td style="padding:6px 10px">tokens per parameter</td>
      <td style="padding:6px 10px; text-align:right; font-weight:600">${preCalc.perParam.toFixed(1)}${
        preCalc.perParam < 20 ? " — under Chinchilla" : ""
      }</td></tr>
</table>`
```

Three settings worth typing in.

**8B parameters, 15,000B tokens, 14% MFU** reproduces Llama 3.1 8B. The table
reads **1.44M GPU-hours** against the **1.46M** Meta published — the last 1.4%
is the slider's integer step (13.9% would land on the nose) and the fact that
the real model has 8.03B parameters, not 8.00B. Close enough that you can
trust the tool.

**405B and 15,600B at 35%** reproduces the flagship: 30.42M GPU-hours against
a published 30.84M. Nudge the MFU slider down one step to **34.5%** — the
effective figure we computed two sections ago — and it reads 30.86M, which is
the published number. That is the whole trick: [once you know a run's real
MFU, four multiplications reproduce its invoice]{.hl}.

**10B and 200B at 35%** is a serious academic run — 20.0 tokens per parameter,
exactly Chinchilla-optimal, for about **9,600 GPU-hours** and **\$24,000** at
\$2.50/hour. Now drop the fleet from 512 to **64**, which is closer to what a
well-funded university lab actually owns, and watch the wall clock go from
under a day to **6.3 days**. Then raise the tokens until it stops being
acceptable. That last step is the real lesson: [the binding constraint is
almost never the FLOPs, it is the calendar]{.hl}.

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**The H200 option is deliberately a no-op.** Look at the code: it computes the
same 989 TFLOP/s as the H100, so picking it changes nothing. That is not a
bug. Per NVIDIA's own datasheets the two chips have identical BF16 tensor-core
throughput; what differs is memory — **80 GB at 3.35 TB/s** on the H100 versus
**141 GB of HBM3e at 4.8 TB/s** on the H200. An H200 buys you bigger batches
and longer contexts without sharding as hard, which shows up as a *better
achievable MFU*, not as more peak FLOP/s. So if you want to model one, leave
the accelerator alone and raise the MFU slider instead.

[Memory capacity and memory bandwidth are what you are usually short of, not
arithmetic]{.hl} — and that is a lesson this calculator structurally cannot
teach you, because $6ND$ does not know memory exists. Keep it in mind every
time a formula in this chapter gives you a clean answer.
:::

### Who actually followed Chinchilla?

@sec-scaling-laws gave the compute-optimal ratio: about 20 tokens per
parameter [@hoffmann2022chinchilla]. Nobody shipping a model obeys it.

| model | tokens per parameter |
|:--|--:|
| GPT-3 175B | 1.7 |
| Chinchilla 70B | 20.0 |
| Llama 3.1 405B | 38.5 |
| Llama 3.1 70B | 212.5 |
| Llama 3.1 8B | 1,868.0 |

GPT-3 sits an order of magnitude *below* the line, which is exactly the
finding Chinchilla was published to correct — it was badly undertrained. Every
Llama sits above it, and the small models sit absurdly above it: the 8B saw
almost **1,900 tokens per parameter**, ninety-three times what compute-optimal
training would recommend.

This is not a mistake and it is not fashion. It is a different optimisation
with a different objective.

### Train once, serve forever

Chinchilla minimises the cost of *reaching* a given loss. If you are going to
serve the model, that is the wrong objective, because training is paid once
and inference is paid on every request until the model is retired.

The arithmetic is short. Generating one token costs about $2N$ FLOPs — the
forward pass only, no backward. So for Llama 3.1 8B:

$$
\underbrace{7.23\times10^{23}}_{\text{training}} \;\Big/\;
\underbrace{1.61\times10^{10}}_{\text{per generated token}} \;=\; 4.5\times10^{13}
$$

[Forty-five trillion generated tokens, and the serving FLOPs have equalled the
training FLOPs.]{.hl} A service producing 100 billion tokens a day passes that
point in 450 days. Any product with real usage crosses it.

Say what that point is and is not. It is FLOP parity for *one* model: the moment
its lifetime inference has cost as much arithmetic as its training. It is not
the point at which extra pretraining pays for itself, because training the same
model on more tokens does not lower its inference cost per token — the parameter
count does that. The break-even that answers "should we have trained longer" is
between two models $A$ and $B$ of *equal quality*:
$T_{\text{break}} = (\text{Train}_A - \text{Train}_B)/(\text{Serve}_B - \text{Serve}_A)$
per token, which is the calculation that makes a smaller, longer-trained model
worth its extra training run. And the build-versus-buy question is a third
thing again, comparing training plus deployment plus operations against an API
invoice.

**And 45 trillion is the most favourable number you will ever get.** It
compares FLOPs to FLOPs, which quietly assumes a generated token and a trained
token cost the same to produce. They do not, for two reasons that both push
the same way:

- *Decode is memory-bound, not compute-bound.* Generating one token at a time
  means reading the entire weight matrix out of memory to do a single small
  matrix-vector product. Training reads those same weights once and amortises
  them over thousands of tokens in a batch. Where pretraining sustains 35–40%
  MFU, decode typically runs at a few percent — the chip is waiting on memory,
  not computing.
- *Prefill is free in this formula and is not free in life.* Every *input*
  token also costs $2N$, and most real workloads send far more input than they
  receive back. A long system prompt, a retrieved document, a chat history: all
  paid for, none of it counted above.

Redo the comparison in GPU-hours instead of FLOPs — the thing you actually
rent — against the 8B's published 1.46M H100-hours:

| decode efficiency | break-even | at 100B tokens/day |
|:--|--:|--:|
| 13.9% MFU | 45.0T tokens | 15 months |
| 10% MFU (large batches, well tuned) | 32.4T tokens | 11 months |
| 5% MFU | 16.2T tokens | 5 months |
| 2% MFU (typical interactive serving) | 6.5T tokens | **2 months** |

Look at the first row and at the 8B's effective MFU back in the table above.
They are the same 13.9%, and that is not a coincidence: [dividing FLOPs by
FLOPs silently assumes your decode server is exactly as efficient as Meta's
training cluster was]{.hl}. Written down like that, the assumption is obviously
untenable — the whole point of decode is that it cannot batch the way training
does.

So 45 trillion is an upper bound, and the real crossover is somewhere between
a month and a year of serious traffic. Which only sharpens the argument:
overtraining pays back faster than the clean formula suggests, not slower.

That is the whole justification for training an 8B model on 15 trillion
tokens. You spend 93× the compute-optimal budget up front to get a model that
is permanently cheaper to run than the compute-optimal alternative of the same
quality. The bigger, "correct" model would have been cheaper to train and more
expensive forever.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**The same logic decides your build-versus-buy question.** Work out your
expected tokens per day, multiply by the model's $2N$, and compare to what
that model cost to make. If you are three orders of magnitude below
break-even, you are a rounding error in someone else's inference fleet and you
should be renting, not training. Most teams are.
:::

## The model landscape {#sec-model-landscape}

Everything so far explains why there are perhaps a dozen organisations on
earth doing stage 1 at frontier scale, and why the rest of us are choosing
among their outputs. So: how do you tell those outputs apart?

Not by the word "open". [A release is not open or closed; it is a set of four
independent decisions]{.hl}, and vendors mix them freely.

:::: {.anlp-fig}
```{=html}
<div class="fig-title">Four things a release can open, decided separately</div>
<svg viewBox="0 0 764 336" style="max-width:744px" role="img"
     aria-label="A grid with three rows of release type and four columns of what is disclosed. The columns are weights, training data, training code, and whether the licence is a standard open-source licence. API-only releases such as GPT-4, Claude and Gemini disclose none of the four. Open-weights releases such as Llama 3.1, Qwen 2.5 and Mistral publish the weights but not the training data or the training code, and their licences vary: Qwen 2.5 and Mistral 7B ship under Apache 2.0, while Llama 3.1 uses custom terms with conditions. Fully open releases such as OLMo 2 and Pythia publish all four, including the training corpus and an Apache 2.0 licence. The caption notes that the middle row is where almost every practical decision is made.">
```
