::: {.fig-cap}
The columns are independent. A release can publish weights and withhold data;
it can use a permissive licence on a model nobody can reproduce. "Open" alone
tells you nothing about which.
:::
::::

### What each column buys you

**Weights** buy you deployment. Given them — this is what makes something an
[open-weights model](#gloss-open-weights-model){#term-open-weights-model .term-ref} — you can run it on your own hardware, in
your own country, with no request leaving your network, which for a Turkish
institution subject to KVKK is frequently the entire argument. You can also
fine-tune, quantize, and inspect activations.

::: {#gloss-open-weights-model .column-margin .term-gloss}
**open-weights model** — one whose trained parameters you can download and run yourself. It says nothing about whether the training data, the training code, or a permissive licence came with them; those are three separate questions. [↩](#term-open-weights-model){.term-back}
:::

**Training data** buys you audit. Without it you cannot check whether your
evaluation set leaked into training [@oren2024proving; @magar2022data], cannot
tell whether your language was represented, cannot answer a lawyer asking
where the text came from [@longpre2024audit], and cannot investigate a
memorised passage that turns up in production.

**Training code** buys you reproduction and, more usefully, *modification* —
being able to run the recipe on your own corpus rather than starting from a
paper.

**The licence** buys you the right to do all of the above in a product. This
is the column that most often surprises people, because "open weights" and
"open source" are routinely used as synonyms and are not.

It is also the column that varies *within* a row, which is why the diagram
says "varies" rather than picking a symbol. All three models named in the
middle row publish weights and withhold data and code — but Qwen 2.5 and
Mistral 7B are released under plain **Apache 2.0**, the same licence the fully
open models use, while Llama 3.1 carries **custom terms**. [Two releases can
be identical on three columns and differ completely on the fourth]{.hl}, so
there is no shortcut here: you have to check the specific model.

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**Read the licence before the benchmark table.** The Llama 3.1 Community
Licence is permissive for nearly everyone and is not an open-source licence.
Three concrete conditions, from the licence text itself:

- if your product had **more than 700 million monthly active users** in the
  month before the release date, you must request a separate licence from
  Meta, which Meta "may grant … in its sole discretion";
- you must display **"Built with Llama"** and ship a copy of the agreement;
- any model you train or improve using Llama outputs must have a name that
  **begins with "Llama"**.

None of those will stop a university project or most companies. All of them
are conditions that an OSI-approved licence such as Apache 2.0 does not
impose, which is exactly why the distinction has a name. OLMo, by contrast,
releases code and weights under Apache 2.0 along with its pretraining corpus
Dolma [@groeneveld2024olmo; @soldaini2024dolma] — and its successors have kept
that commitment.
:::

The fully-open row exists for a reason that matters more to a university than
to a startup: [it is the row on which controlled replication and ablation are
straightforward.]{.hl} If you want to
ask "does adding Turkish data at 5% help or hurt English?", you need the data
and the code, not just the weights. The Pile [@gao2020pile], RefinedWeb
[@penedo2023refinedweb], Dolma [@soldaini2024dolma], and FineWeb
[@penedo2024fineweb] exist so that question can be asked at all.

### Reading a model card critically {#sec-model-cards}

A [model card](#gloss-model-card){#term-model-card .term-ref} is a short structured document describing what a model is, what
it was trained on, and where it should not be used [@mitchell2019model]; the
same idea applied to datasets is a datasheet [@gebru2021datasheets]. They are
now standard, which means they are now marketing as well as documentation.
Read them the way you would read a drug label: the useful information is
specific, and the interesting information is what has been left out.

::: {#gloss-model-card .column-margin .term-gloss}
**model card** — the document a lab publishes alongside a model, stating its intended use, training data, evaluation results, and limitations. Voluntary, unaudited, and still the most useful page you will read about a model. [↩](#term-model-card){.term-back}
:::

Work through Llama 3.1's card, which is better than most, and the technique
becomes clear.

| what the card says | how to read it |
|:--|:--|
| "15T+ tokens" in the table, "~15 trillion" in the prose | a floor and an approximation, on one page. The paper's 15.6T is the real one |
| "cutoff of December 2023" | hard, checkable, and the single most useful line on the card |
| supported languages: English, German, French, Italian, Portuguese, Hindi, Spanish, Thai | **Turkish is not on the list** |
| "trained on a broader collection of languages than the 8 supported" | so the list is a *support* boundary, not a capability measurement |
| "11,390 tons CO2eq" location-based, "0 tons" market-based | one run, two accounting standards, both true |
| benchmark tables | the model was tuned while these were visible; treat as an upper bound |

The language row is the one to sit with. The card puts use "in languages
beyond those explicitly referenced" **out of scope** — and yet our own
measurement two sections ago found Llama 3's tokenizer handling Turkish at
1.23× English, better than any other multilingual tokenizer tested. Both
statements are accurate. The card is telling you what Meta will stand behind,
not what the model can do.

[That gap is the whole reason you measure.]{.hl} A card cannot tell you
whether a model is good at *your* task in *your* language, because the vendor
did not evaluate that. For Turkish, nobody is going to do this for you.

Four questions no card answers, which you should therefore ask yourself:

1. **Was my evaluation set in the training data?** You usually cannot know.
   Assume contamination on any public benchmark older than the model, and keep
   a private held-out set [@kapoor2023leakage; @oren2024proving].
2. **How much of my language was in there?** Llama 3's 8% multilingual slice
   is shared across dozens of languages. Assume small.
3. **What does the model do at the boundary of its documented scope?** Test
   it. That is what @sec-llm-eval is for.
4. **What happens when this model is deprecated?** For an API, the answer may
   be "your prompts stop working on a schedule you do not control". For open
   weights, the answer is "nothing", and that is a real feature with a real
   price.

### Choosing one, in practice

The decision has four inputs and they are usually considered in the wrong
order. Capability first is the wrong order, because capability is the
constraint you are least likely to bind on and the most expensive to
over-buy.

Ask them like this instead:

1. **Where is the data allowed to be?** If personal data cannot leave the
   country or the building, the API row is gone and no benchmark score brings
   it back. Decide this first; it eliminates more options than anything else.
2. **What does the licence permit?** Check the user-count clause, the naming
   clause, and the attribution clause against your actual product. Do this
   second, while it is still cheap to change your mind.
3. **What can you afford to serve?** From the arithmetic above: $2N$ FLOPs per
   generated token. Multiply by your expected traffic. This usually chooses
   your parameter count for you, and it usually chooses something smaller than
   you assumed.
4. **Only now, is it good enough?** Evaluate the survivors on *your* data.
   The public leaderboard is a screening tool at best, and after contamination
   it is barely that.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**The default that is right more often than it should be.** Start with the
smallest open-weights model that clears your quality bar on your own
evaluation set, and treat a frontier API as the thing you escalate to for the
hard tail of requests. It is cheaper, it is private, it does not change under
you, and — from the break-even arithmetic above — the economics improve every
month your traffic grows. @sec-serving takes this apart properly.
:::

## Lab: price a Turkish pretraining run {#sec-pretraining-lab}

Everything in this lab is arithmetic and tokenizer calls. Nothing here needs a
GPU — which is the point, because the decision this chapter is about gets made
long before anyone touches a GPU.

1. **Measure fertility on your own text.** Take 2,000–5,000 sentences of
   Turkish from a domain you care about — support tickets, legal text, news,
   clinical notes, your own thesis. Tokenize with at least four tokenizers:
   one English-first (`openai-community/gpt2`), two multilingual
   (`NousResearch/Meta-Llama-3-8B`, `Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B`), and one Turkish-native
   (`dbmdz/bert-base-turkish-cased`). Those are the exact identifiers behind
   the table in @sec-tokenizer-budget, so your numbers should reproduce ours
   on the same corpus. Report tokens-per-word and total tokens for each. Do
   **not** report tokens-per-word alone as a cross-language claim; you now
   know why.
2. **Get the honest ratio.** Translate — or find an existing parallel
   version of — 200 of those sentences into English. Recompute the ratio on
   matched content. State how far your domain's number is from this chapter's
   1.23× for Llama 3, and give one concrete reason for the gap. Domain
   vocabulary is the usual culprit: proper nouns, code, numbers and acronyms
   tokenize almost identically in both languages and drag the ratio toward 1.
3. **Turn the ratio into money.** Pick a real API price list. Compute what
   one million of your Turkish documents costs to process under each
   tokenizer's ratio. Then compute the same figure for the English
   translations. The difference is the surcharge, in your currency, for your
   product.
4. **Find the context ceiling.** For a 128K-token context window, compute how
   many Turkish *words* fit under each tokenizer, and how many English words
   fit. Report both. This is the number that decides whether a document fits
   in one @sec-retrieval chunk or three.
5. **Budget a run with $C = 6ND$.** Suppose you want a Turkish-first base
   model. Choose $N$ and $D$ yourself and justify both: $N$ from what you
   intend to serve (@sec-serving), $D$ from what Turkish text actually exists
   at the quality you need. Use the calculator in @sec-pretraining-compute to
   get FLOPs, GPU-hours, wall-clock on a fleet you could plausibly rent, and a
   dollar figure. Then state your assumed MFU and defend it — if you wrote
   down a number above 40%, say which paper you are matching.
6. **Sanity-check against reality.** Compare your budget to the three
   published Llama 3.1 runs. If your number is far smaller, find the
   assumption doing the work. It is almost always MFU or the token count.
7. **Now do the sensitivity analysis.** Recompute the run's cost with 1.23×
   more tokens — the Turkish surcharge applied to the *training* corpus, not
   just inference. Report the extra dollars. Then answer the question the
   number poses: at what point does it become cheaper to train a Turkish
   tokenizer and a smaller model than to pay the surcharge on a multilingual
   one forever?
8. **Compute your own break-even, twice.** Using $2N$ FLOPs per generated
   token, find how many tokens your service must generate before serving
   costs exceed training. That is the FLOP-parity answer, and you now know it
   is an upper bound. So do it again in GPU-hours, assuming decode sustains
   2–5% MFU against your training run's 35%. Convert both to months at your
   projected traffic. If the honest answer is under a year, you have just
   discovered why inference-optimal and compute-optimal are different
   objectives.

**Deliverable:** a one-page memo — the kind you would actually send — that
recommends *train*, *fine-tune*, or *use an API* for a specific Turkish
product, with the fertility table, the compute budget, and the break-even
month as its three pieces of evidence. State the assumption that, if wrong,
would flip your recommendation.

## Intuition checks {#sec-pretraining-intuition}

Answer before expanding. Each is a place where the intuitive answer is wrong in
a direction that costs money — which is the recurring theme of pretraining
decisions you inherit and cannot undo.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 1. Turkish needs 1.59 tokens per word and English needs 1.28. Does Turkish cost more?

Not with that tokenizer, and the comparison is invalid as posed.

Tokens-per-word compares units of different size. Turkish is agglutinative:
*evlerinizden* is one word meaning "from your houses". [The honest measurement
is tokens for the *same content*]{.hl} — tokenize a sentence and its
professional translation and divide.

Do that on 1,157 aligned pairs and BERTurk costs **0.58×** what English costs;
the Turkish-native tokenizers are the only ones where Turkish is *cheaper*.
GPT-2 costs **1.98×**, Llama 3 and multilingual BERT **1.23×**.

The same corpus is 8,058 Turkish words against 10,862 English words of matched
content — the agglutination is visible in the raw counts before any tokenizer
touches it.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 2. Your model tokenizes Turkish badly. Can you fine-tune your way out of it?

Not with an ordinary fine-tune, and that is why the tokenizer belongs in a
pretraining chapter rather than a preprocessing one.

Changing the tokenizer changes the embedding table, which changes every weight
downstream. It is not impossible: you can extend the vocabulary, initialise the
new embeddings from the pieces they replace, and continue pretraining until the
model settles — a documented and occasionally worthwhile procedure, and
vocabulary-adaptation methods exist that initialise the new rows from the old
ones rather than from scratch. What it is not is free or safe. Its cost scales
with how much of the vocabulary you change, what you start from and what quality
you will accept, and it risks degrading things the model already does well; it
is not automatically a second pretraining run, and it is not an ordinary
fine-tune either. [The tokenizer is how the compute budget gets divided between
languages, and undoing that division is a project with its own budget.]{.hl}
Absent
that project, a user of a 1.98× tokenizer pays the surcharge in context window,
in latency, and on every API invoice, for the life of the model.

Llama 3 shows the decision being made deliberately: 100,000 tokens from
`tiktoken` plus **28,000 added specifically for non-English languages**,
reported as improving compression for those languages with no cost to English.
That is a design choice with a price tag, made once, before the first gradient
step.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 3. A vendor quotes 40% MFU. Is that good?

Unanswerable until you ask what went in the denominator, and asking is the
whole point of the question.

The same GPU has a dense peak and a sparsity peak twice as large, and the
denominator decides the answer: dividing by the larger one *halves* the
reported MFU. Llama 3's Table 4 reports 430 TFLOP/s per GPU; against the H100's
dense BF16 peak that is $430/989 = 43.5\%$, and against the 2:4-sparsity peak
the same run reports $430/1{,}979 = 21.7\%$. The 43.5% confirms they used the
dense figure. Two MFUs are comparable only when they used the same peak, and
nobody is obliged to tell you which they used.

The second trap is the numerator. Reconstructing Llama 3.1 405B from $6ND$
alone gives 34.5%; adding the attention term gives **36.0–37.1%**, which brackets the **36.9%** our illustrative 41% × 0.90 estimate predicts. [$6ND$ omits attention, which is fine for a
budget estimate and not fine for a utilization comparison.]{.hl}

Two numbers that look comparable and are not is the most common way engineering
conversations about efficiency go wrong.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 4. Where does the 6 in $C = 6ND$ come from?

Three twos, each with a cause, and knowing them is what lets you adapt the
formula instead of reciting it.

Two FLOPs per parameter in the **forward** pass, because each weight
participates in one multiply and one add. Two more for the **backward pass
through the inputs**, because the error has to keep travelling to earlier
layers. Two more for the **backward pass through the weights**, because the
optimiser needs to know what to change.

So the forward pass is $2ND$ and is only a third of the bill — which
immediately tells you that inference costs roughly $2N$ FLOPs *per token*
(hence $2ND$ for $D$ tokens), not $6N$, and that is the number that decides whether serving or training dominates your
budget. It also tells you why $6ND$ is a *pretraining* law and does not
transfer unchanged to fine-tuning with frozen weights.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 5. You have more compute. Should you train a bigger model or use more data?

Both, in roughly equal measure — and the interesting part is that this was the
field's mistake for two years.

Chinchilla's finding is that parameters and tokens should scale together;
earlier models were badly undertrained for their size. But the compute-optimal
answer is not the answer you want if you are going to *serve* the model:
[a smaller model trained longer costs more to train and less to run
forever]{.hl}, which is why production models are routinely trained well past
the compute-optimal point.

The lab's break-even question is the practical form: if your model serves for
more than a few months, inference-optimal and compute-optimal are different
objectives and the one you should be optimising is inference-optimal, not
compute-optimal.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 6. Can you just train on the same data twice instead of collecting more?

Up to a point that is measurable and then not.

Muennighoff et al. found repeated data "yields negligible changes to loss
compared to having unique data" for the first few epochs, and degrades sharply
after. Roughly four epochs is the region where a repeated token is still worth
close to a fresh one; past that you are spending compute to memorise.

The practical reading for a language like Turkish: [the constraint on a
Turkish pretraining run is the corpus, not the GPUs]{.hl}, and repetition buys
you a small multiple rather than an escape. That is also why the data-filtering
decisions in @sec-pretraining-data get so much attention — when you cannot get
more text, what you keep matters much more.
:::

## Interview questions {#sec-pretraining-interview}

Pretraining questions are rarely about whether you would run one. They are
about whether you can reason quantitatively about a system you inherited, which
is the actual job.

::: {.column-margin}
Almost nobody being interviewed has pretrained a model, and the interviewer
knows it. What separates answers is whether you can do the arithmetic that
decides *build, fine-tune, or buy* — and whether you know which pretraining
decisions you are stuck with afterwards.
:::

1. **Estimate the compute for a 7B model on 2 trillion tokens.** $C \approx 6ND
   = 6 \times 7\times10^9 \times 2\times10^{12} \approx 8.4\times10^{22}$
   FLOPs. Then convert to something a budget-holder understands: divide by the
   per-GPU throughput you actually expect — not peak, roughly 40% of dense peak
   — times 3,600 seconds, and you have GPU-hours. Say out loud that $6ND$
   ignores attention, which is a few percent at short context and much more at
   long, and that [the thing that actually blows up a pretraining schedule is
   almost never the FLOPs, it is the calendar]{.hl}: interruptions, restarts and
   checkpoint reloads.

2. **What is the single pretraining decision you cannot undo later?** The
   tokenizer. Everything else — instruction behaviour, safety, domain
   knowledge, even a good deal of factual content — can be moved by
   post-training (@sec-post-training). The tokenizer is the one that resists,
   because changing it means rebuilding the embedding table the rest of the
   weights were trained against — possible, but a project rather than a
   fine-tune. Quantify the
   stakes with the fertility table: a Turkish user on GPT-2's tokenizer pays
   **1.98×** the tokens of an English user for the same content, and on BERTurk
   **0.58×**. Same language, same text, a 3.4× spread driven entirely by a
   decision made before training started.

3. **How would you decide whether to pretrain, fine-tune, or use an API for a
   Turkish product?** Three numbers, in this order. Fertility, because it sets
   your per-token cost forever and may by itself justify a Turkish-native model.
   The $6ND$ budget for the smallest model that could work, which is almost
   always large enough to end the conversation. And the break-even month: the
   point where API spend at your projected traffic exceeds training plus
   serving. If break-even is under a year, you have discovered that
   inference-optimal and compute-optimal are different objectives. The answer
   for nearly every product is *fine-tune or buy* — being able to show *why*
   with arithmetic is the skill.

4. **Where does pretraining data actually come from, and what is thrown away?**
   Common Crawl or a cleaned derivative such as FineWeb, and the honest headline
   is how much is discarded: filtering, deduplication and quality classification
   remove the large majority of raw crawl. Name the specific steps — boilerplate
   removal, language identification, deduplication across crawls, quality
   classifiers — and the counter-intuitive finding that FineWeb's authors hit:
   aggressive deduplication across *all* crawls made things worse, because it
   preferentially kept the low-quality text that had not been repeated.
   [Deduplication is not monotonically good]{.hl}, which is the kind of detail
   that shows you read the report rather than the summary.

5. **A model claims a 128K context window. What should you be sceptical about?**
   That the quality is uniform across it, and that you can afford it. On
   quality, training rarely happens at full length throughout — the context is
   usually extended in stages near the end — so the last 100K tokens have seen
   far less training than the first 8K. On cost, take @sec-attention-cost's
   arithmetic: with plain multi-head attention a 7B model's KV cache at 100,000 tokens is
   52.4 GB per concurrent request, against 14 GB of weights — but with the
   grouped-query attention every current 8B model uses (8 KV heads instead of
   32) the same cache is 13.1 GB. A 4× difference out of one line of config. The window being *advertised*
   and the window being *usable at your budget* are different numbers.

6. **Why do small pretraining runs look so much less efficient than large
   ones?** Because efficiency here is mostly about keeping an accelerator busy,
   and small models give it less to work with: less arithmetic per unit of
   communication, less work to hide latency behind. Reconstructed MFU for
   Llama 3.1 goes 15.8–17.2% at 8B, 27.4–29.0% at 70B, 36.0–37.1% at 405B. Then
   add the caveat that makes the answer honest: published GPU-hours are
   *allocated* hours including evaluation, checkpointing and idle time, and only
   the 405B has a published MFU to check against — so treat the 8B figure as an
   upper bound on waste rather than a measurement of kernel quality.

## Where to go deeper

Two things are worth doing before reading any of the papers. Open
[FineWeb's interactive report](https://huggingface.co/spaces/HuggingFaceFW/blogpost-fineweb-v1)
and read the ablation plots — it is the rare case where a lab published the
failed variants alongside the shipped one. Then open the
[tokenizer playground](https://huggingface.co/spaces/Xenova/the-tokenizer-playground)
and paste in the longest Turkish word you know; the whole of
@sec-tokenizer-budget becomes obvious in about ten seconds.

Then watch someone do it: Karpathy's
[Let's reproduce GPT-2 (124M)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=l8pRSuU81PU)
is four hours of actual pretraining, which makes every number in this chapter
concrete, and
[Stanford CS336](https://stanford-cs336.github.io/spring2025/) is a whole
course built around doing it yourself.

The papers below are the ones this chapter's numbers came from. Read them in
roughly this order:

| topic | source |
|:--|:--|
| a full pretraining run, documented | @grattafiori2024llama3 |

## Exercises

1. Take one open model card and one closed model card. List three claims each
   makes that you could verify yourself, and three you cannot. Then state
   which of the six unverifiable claims would most change your decision if it
   turned out to be false.
2. The FineWeb team tested global deduplication with a pointed experiment.
   Inside the single old 2013-48 snapshot they took the ~31B tokens global
   dedup had **kept** and the ~460B tokens it had **removed** (re-deduplicated
   on their own, giving 171B), trained a model on each, and found the model
   trained on the *removed* data was better. Explain the mechanism — note that
   the experiment compares two slices of one snapshot, not two corpora, which
   is what makes it a clean test. Then name one filter elsewhere in the funnel
   that could fail in exactly the same way, and say what you would measure to
   catch it.
3. Llama 3's final annealing stage covers 40M tokens: 0.00026% of the run. It
   improved GSM8k by **24.0%** on the 8B model — the paper's figure is a
   relative improvement, not a gain in percentage points, and the difference
   matters for how impressed you should be — and by essentially nothing on the
   405B. Give an explanation consistent with both results. Your explanation
   should predict something — say what.
4. A vendor advertises 1,979 TFLOP/s for their accelerator. You measure a
   sustained 310 TFLOP/s on your own training job. Work through the gap in
   three named steps, using this chapter's figures for each, and state what
   fraction of the shortfall you could plausibly recover with better
   engineering versus what is structural.
5. Compute $6ND$ for a 3B model on 2T tokens. Then compute how many H100-hours
   it needs at 40% MFU, and how long that takes on 64 GPUs. Now recompute at
   25% MFU — the figure you should assume for a first run on a cluster nobody
   has tuned. Report both wall-clock numbers and say which one belongs in a
   project plan.
6. Our corpus measurement found Qwen 2.5 (vocab 151,643) tokenizing Turkish
   at 1.40× English, while Llama 3 (vocab 128,000) managed 1.23×. Explain why
   the larger vocabulary lost. Then design the smallest experiment that would
   confirm your explanation, and say what result would refute it.
7. For `evlerinizden`, Llama 3 produces `ev|ler|iniz|den` — four tokens that
   are exactly the four morphemes — while Cosmos GPT-2 produces
   `ev|lerinizden`: two tokens, half the cost, and a second token that is not
   a linguistic unit at all. Argue for each as the better segmentation. Then
   state what you would measure to settle it, and be specific about the task,
   because the answer is not the same for every task.
8. GPT-3 used 1.7 tokens per parameter; Llama 3.1's 8B used 1,868. Both were
   rational decisions. Reconstruct the reasoning behind each, then find the
   traffic level at which GPT-3's ratio would have been the correct choice
   for Meta.
9. You are given a fixed budget of 10,000 H100-hours — a realistic Turkish
   university allocation. Using this chapter's arithmetic, work out the
   largest model you could pretrain from scratch on a Chinchilla-optimal token
   count. Then argue, with numbers, for spending the same allocation on
   continued pretraining of an existing open-weights model instead. State
   which you would actually do and why.
10. Common Crawl's WET extraction "retained too much boilerplate and menu
    text", so FineWeb re-extracted from WARC with trafilatura. Boilerplate is
    highly repetitive. Explain why deduplication does not simply remove it,
    and what that tells you about the order of operations in a data pipeline.
